Newly hatched Ten-spined stickleback larvae emerge from the egg at a remarkably small size, with the standard length at birth measuring 0.63 cm [Lb = 0.63 cm], a value that has been obtained from the closely related three-spined stickleback, Gasterosteus aculeatus, due to the logistical difficulty of observing the precise moment of eclosion in this species. The incubation period prior to this event, during which the yolk-dependent embryo develops within the chorion, lasts approximately 6.5 days [ab = approximately 6.5 days] at a constant water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This brief embryonic phase, typical of small-bodied gasterosteids, results in the emergence of a lecithotrophic larva that remains reliant on its endogenous yolk reserves for a short period before the trophic switch to exogenous feeding begins. The wet weight of these newly emerged prolarvae, calculated from the standard birth length, is estimated to be approximately 0.0028 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0028 grams].

As the yolk-sac larva completes the absorption of its endogenous nutrients and initiates first exogenous feeding, the individual transitions into a free-swimming, actively growing juvenile. Growth during this early phase is rapid, yet the species remains modest in stature throughout its life. Field surveys and laboratory growth studies indicate that the ultimate standard length, representing the maximum size attained by fully grown adults, reaches 7.40 cm [Li = 7.40 cm]. This adult body size is characteristic of the species and distinguishes it from the larger three-spined stickleback with which it sometimes co-occurs. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of a fully developed adult, derived from its maximum length, is calculated to be roughly 4.47 grams [Wwi = roughly 4.47 grams]. This relatively small body mass imposes constraints on the species' metabolic demands and shapes its position within the littoral food web, where it forages primarily on small benthic invertebrates and zooplankton.

The onset of reproductive maturity is marked not by the attainment of maximum body size, but rather by the achievement of a distinct, intermediate standard length. Individuals of this species typically become sexually mature and capable of spawning once they reach a standard length of 3.70 cm [Lp = 3.70 cm]. At this critical developmental threshold, the gonads undergo vitellogenesis and spermiation, marking the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and the transition to a breeding adult. The corresponding wet weight at this pubertal stage, estimated from the length-weight relationship, is approximately 0.56 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.56 grams]. This value is considerably lower than the ultimate body mass, indicating that a substantial portion of somatic growth continues even after the commencement of reproductive activity, a life-history pattern typical of many iteroparous fishes that continue to grow throughout their adult lives.

Reproductive output in this small stickleback is characterized by repeated spawning events over a relatively extended breeding season. Under optimal thermal conditions, experiments conducted at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] have documented that females are capable of producing approximately 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 5 eggs per clutch], with spawning occurring approximately 16 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 16 times per year], yielding a sustained reproductive output that balances the energetic constraints of a small body cavity. The first successful spawning event in the life of a female generally occurs after a considerable period of juvenile growth and gonadal development. Research indicates that the age at first reproduction is 547 days after hatching [tR = 547 days after hatching], a milestone that occurs when the fish are maintained at a stable temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This comparatively late onset of breeding relative to the species' lifespan reflects the time investment needed to reach the critical standard length of 3.70 cm and accumulate sufficient energy reserves.

Longevity records for the Ten-spined stickleback, derived from long-term mark-recapture studies of populations inhabiting cool, stable water bodies, indicate that the maximum lifespan is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] under natural conditions with a mean annual temperature near 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This maximum recorded longevity is typical for a fish of this size and metabolic pace, reflecting the constraints imposed by cold-water environments on cellular maintenance and repair processes. The relatively slow pace of life, characterized by delayed maturation and a moderate reproductive rate, is consistent with populations inhabiting nutrient-poor northern waters. Environmental temperature plays a central role in governing this pace; the extended incubation, the delayed attainment of sexual maturity, and the overall lifespan are all calibrated to the cool thermal regime, typically around 10 °C [T = 10 °C], that dominates the species' native habitats.
